parent: (story) One month without AI
text:
The loudest voices in the tech discourse right now generally argue for software engineering to be either dead or have mutated to something completely different where almost none of the old skills transfers, because now you have to be a designer and the small details don't matter anymore.

Except that every designer worth their salt knows that understanding the small details is a necessary step towards mastering the big picture, and in fact this part is often left unspecified by the techfluencers (how do you become good at design in the first place? certainly not by delegating most decision-making to an LLM).

The big picture (i.e. making software you can love) is what we've been always after in the Zig community, which is why we do things like https://kristoff.it/blog/the-zig-journey/.

In other words my point is that trying to stay one month without AI can do you some good, but IMO the best approach is to have a holistic view of your learning process that doesn't put learning entirely on pause until you take another break from LLMs.

This was always important, but it's even more important now because the software engineering "middle-class" is shrinking and if you don't gain any special insight on how to make excellent quality software, then you are more likely to land in the meat proxy job bucket, from which is going to be increasingly harder to get out as the job market adapts.

author: bartekci
parent: (story) One month without AI
text:
I went back to TDD, to my PRs with just 5 files changed. To my 2-line PR descriptions that were straight to the point. I went back to understanding what I was doing, to deploying with confidence, to being ready for a detailed code review, because I knew what the changes were doing, and I could justify every line of code. I went back to enjoying human code reviews (not AI-ones, I still hate those. Even more humans that paste AI reviews pretending they are their own), to learning from them. I started asking about architectural decisions, why things were a certain way.


The loss of all this is a common theme I'm seeing in the industry and one I am grateful my team has not lost. We use AI to output the code (with human adjustments here and there, but we mostly steer). We have empathy for the human reviewer on the other side and deliver well thought out PRs. We use LLMs to further enhance the PR descriptions with Mermaid diagrams demonstrating the place of that component in the architecture or a flow, but otherwise write every commit message ourselves. We use AI review to catch security concerns and the edge cases humans typically seem to omit, but we still have humans reading each line of code and questioning the bigger architectural understanding. All of our specifications are human written. Most importantly, we all understand the code we're shipping and we feel a strong accountability to it.

I feel we've hit the sweet spot where we're leveraging LLMs to deliver more robust software. Yeah, we're still tired just as everyone in this industry is (no more quiet days crafting code; always focusing on the hard problems), but I'm grateful we have a team that understands that humans still matter.

These two parts are more deeply connected then they might seem at first:


the sorts of practices recommended for maximizing LLM-related gains in the DORA report, and in many other similar whitepapers and reports and studies, are or ought to be as fundamental to software development as hand-washing is to surgery.

[...]

When expressing skepticism about LLM coding, a common response is that not adopting it, or even just delaying slightly in adopting it, will inevitably result in being “left behind”, or even stronger effects (for example, words like “obliterated” have been used, more than once, by acquaintances of mine who really ought to know better). Much has been written about the observed bimodal distribution in programmer compensation, where high-skill programmers make something like 5-20x more than low-skill programmers. If you look at what kinds of projects those different groups produce, you'll see a consistent difference: skilled programmers factor big projects into smaller independently-verifiable submodules, write tests that provide good coverage of important branches, and use tooling (static types, linters) to automate trivial verification. Low-skill programmers do few or none of these things, so they spend a lot of time writing cross-cutting changes and then struggling to manually verify whether they're correct.

LLMs introduce a new capability: given a defined scope and a clear goal the computer can independently iterate toward a solution. The properties that make a project easy for humans to reason about (small scope, good tests, quick error ascription) also make LLMs work faster. In a well-maintained codebase an LLM can offload a truly surprising amount of tedious work, which makes skilled developers both more productive and happier -- more thinking, less carpal tunnel.

LLMs also have a new price point, which is the problem. If you are a programmer who can write code as well as an unguided LLM then as of about six months ago your labor is worth less than $0.50/hr. There are a lot of professional programmers out there who do not write code as well as Claude, and it is correct to describe their mid-term career prospects as "obliterated". Their only hope of staying employed as a programmer is to learn how to effectively use LLMs, and they need to be doing it today.


This quote from Brooks:



There is no single development, in either technology or management technique, which by itself promises even a single order-of-magnitude improvement within a decade in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity.



has, I think, been proven wrong by history. Compilers and automatic memory management can both be credited with at least an order of magnitude in all three metrics, not necessarily immediately (early compilers were buggy, early GCs were slow) but over time. If you don't believe me then ask a junior engineer to write a web service in Python and then write it again in x86-64 assembly.

It's still very early in the development of LLMs (ChatGPT was released less than four years ago!), but even now LLMs seem to be at least as effective as compilers when it comes to shifting human attention "up the stack" towards high-level design vs low-level implementation:


Gemma 4 on a three-year-old GPU can fill in simple TODO stub functions while I'm at lunch. I only need to decide on the type signatures.

Gemini Flash can fill in an entire file of TODO stub functions of arbitrary size, and fix any linter/compiler errors that arise, within 30 seconds. I only need to decide on the type signatures of the public API.

Claude can take a brief human-written language spec plus a few examples and turn it into a correct ABNF grammar, then generate test cases guided by that grammar and LCOV.


If this technology doesn't lead to improved productivity in an organization then they're either doing something extremely specialized or their development process is a mess.

One of the challenges there is the tradeoff between memory management and data locality -- if I use a language like Java or Go with GC then it's very easy to represent the IR as a graph of instructions and operands, but the result is too slow for interactive use on large functions. So I'm writing it in Rust with patterns like "replace pointers with u32 indexes into a Vec<Inst>", and the resulting binary has great performance but the code is way more complicated. The compression algorithm is because I have another project where I need to keep the data file size down, so it needs to be compressed. The modern choices are zstd and lzma but both of those have their main implementations in C, which means I would need to learn how this language's FFI works. If I choose gzip then the compression ratio is lower but there's already a native implementation available. I could also use WebAssembly as a generic embedding mechanism, but the performance is pretty bad even with the complex JIT runtimes.

This is all accidental complexity. It's tedious and repetitive and it's not what I find enjoyable about programming.

The article reads like the author is trying to convince themselves. There's really nothing new here that hasn't been said many times before. The whole argument rests on a false antithesis. To say that because the machine does not do everything by itself, or because it still requires human supervision, it is therefore not useful, is to ignore the whole development of modern software development. Even when the LLM has not sufficient intelligence to carry through an entire process, it may carry through a large number of the nitty-gritty and annoying details involved. It handles syntax quirks, locates library APIs, traces through code, writes boilerplate, and so on. All these things are tedious, and no one ever wants to do them. With an LLM they can be done much more quickly even though the human still makes the final decision.

The author heavily leands on Fred Brooks and the concept of accidental complexity. But they miss the irony entirely. Digging through archaic documentation to find a specific method, or setting up HTTP handlers is the very definition of incidental complexity. Removing that friction allows you to focus on the problem you're actually trying to solve.

In this way the production of software is, in fact, far more accessible. Spending a few months learning how to use an LLM effectively is nothing like spending years learning algorithms, data structures, and design patterns. Building basic programs no longer requires the study of computer science at a level comparable to that of the professional programmer.

I'd argue the fact that people who've never done software development in their live before can now have an LLM whip up a program for them is already is, in fact, a revolutionary development. I can give you a concrete example here. I have a friend who was a Windows user. He's a designer and always found Linux to be too intimidating to switch over to. I helped him get set up with DeepSeek and opencode, and he's been able to solve every problem he's run into using the tool. If he doesn't know how to do something on Linux, or he needs to figure out why something isn't working, or make a script, the LLM solves the problem for him. He's been using Linux for about half a year now without any complaints. For him, this is a revolutionary thing, as he was able to make a jump to Linux which was simply not worth doing before.

Of course, the LLM can't write large scale software on its own, and you need humans in the loop for that. But even there, I'd argue the changes are revolutionary as well. For example, I've never worked with frontend development using Js. I had to work with React and build a frontend recently for a non-trivial app. This is something I just wouldn't have been able to do previously. I know how to structure applications, what good architecture looks like, and so on. But I simply don't have the experience with the specific stack, I don't know the language quirks, the libraries, or the tooling. This would've been months of work to internalize previously. The LLM papered right over all that for me. I was able to use Js just as easily as the languages I'm well versed in. Externalizing experience that used to take many months, or years to develop, into a tool is absolutely revolutionary.

I also disagree with the claim that the limitations of LLMs require some sort of a breakthrough to overcome. The approach may simply lie in better tooling. We already have languages that allow doing formal proofs and contracts. It could be that we simply move in that direction. The human writes a declarative spec for the functionality they want, and the LLM has to figure out how to fill that spec. I linked that Paul Ford article from my post. I also think it's actually a really strong argument for my position.

Back when that article first went up, I posted on social media (initially on Mastodon, but cross-posted to Bluesky where I know you follow me), about how nothing in that article really felt new or groundbreaking to me: that quick data converter is the kind of thing I used to do at the Journal-World back in the day, and that you used to do, too. We could quickly bang out these kinds of projects already, twenty-plus years ago.

Paul Ford's analysis of how long it would take and how much it would cost to do a bespoke data converter at his former company isn't based on the time or cost of producing code, it's based on delivering that software in a different environment, where that project has to be justified and prioritized and documented and have a spec and acceptance criteria and a testing plan and all the other bits.

To go back to the story I posted on Mastodon/Bluesky: if I went to the teams I work with today and showed them the same crime data set the reporter brought down to me in the News Center basement twenty years ago and asked them to build the same online feature for it, the coding time for it would probably be a little bit faster, thanks to advances in tools over the years. But the project would need to be thought through, and prioritized against other projects competing for resources, and have a specification written, and acceptance criteria, and a testing plan, and all the other bits. It would take a lot longer than two days. But the coding, even if done 100% by hand by humans, would still go very quickly. What wouldn't go quickly, and what an LLM can't make go quickly, is all the other bits.

And as much as it would feel great to just go off and build whatever I feel like building whenever I feel like it, I know from experience that in most environments having processes is important, even if it thwarts me on occasion. For example: there's a project at my day job that I've wanted to get built for a while. Writing the code is maybe an hour or two of work, without involving an LLM. I don't need any help prototyping it, I know exactly how it needs to work, and I've built things like it before. The sticking point is that it would replace a pretty critical existing component that a whole bunch of things rely on, and replacing that requires notifying and getting buy-in from a lot of people, and a migration plan, and a fallback plan, and coordinating the switchover with people watching to make sure it goes smoothly, and... well, it doesn't matter how much faster I could write that code with an LLM. An LLM could literally magically reduce the coding time to zero and still not make much of a meaningful dent in the overall end-to-end time to deliver the project, because the coding is not the bottleneck.

It's also not the bottleneck for Paul Ford. He knows that. You know that. I know you both know that.

That is a great question I genuinely had not thought about. After some checking, it turns out it mostly does affect date formatting appropriate for each locale. Some gaps, still looking into it.

But yes, it does more than the strings. Dates go through a per-locale table, so it's 8/3/2026 in English, 03.08.2026 in German and Czech, 2026/8/3 in Japanese, 2026-08-03 in Swedish. I'll be following up to find other gaps and address them. The hard problem for me is always that I don't know that language or culture or whether they use commas as separators or periods, etc.

This is the sort of problem I had serious experience with at my last job. Our Ruby currency gem hadn't been updated in 13 years, and it still treated the yen as having subunits. I must have gone through a dozen comment section solutions for my personal blog before realizing what I really wanted doesn't exist: no bloat, no ads, no tracking, no third-party embed, etc, and the comments end up as part of my own site the next time it builds. Well, «small independent blog hosting» which you more or less offer can only be small and independent if there are many «yet another» ones in this niche!

Right, interpolations are in the active-posting side, which I did not look into as a not-really-user.

As for carrier-noun: I can confirm that in a completely single-language setup, when generating documents, we went to great editing lengths to make sure all proper nouns are in the absolute form (also known as nominative case) and the text is not too broken. I do not believe there is any other solution that scales even within one language. Once you have mutually unintelligible space labels, and the need to the users to understand the link role if not the space name, even more so. Hopefully, you need only one interpolation per sentence, so the carrier-noun setup should work fine without special tricks.

… I only hope your LLM of choice doesn't accidentally translate «your people» into some language in a way that sounds a bit nationalist…
